PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 80 — Lesson 104: Low Back Pain Management

FNP-level goal: Evaluate low back pain safely, identify serious pathology and neurologic emergencies, choose testing only when it answers a clinical question, support functional recovery, and use individualized nonpharmacologic, pharmacologic, and referral strategies.

Learning Objectives

  • Classify low back pain as nonspecific, radicular, spinal-stenosis pattern, or possible serious underlying condition.
  • Recognize cauda equina syndrome, progressive neurologic deficit, infection, fracture, malignancy, and other red flags requiring urgent escalation.
  • Use focused history and examination to select imaging and laboratory testing appropriately rather than routinely.
  • Incorporate function, goals, psychosocial risk factors, and nonpharmacologic care into management.
  • Apply medication and opioid safety principles and know when rehabilitation, pain, spine, or emergency referral is needed.

Part 1 — Start With a Safety Classification

Low back pain is common, but the FNP’s first job is not to name a degenerative finding—it is to determine whether there is a dangerous cause or serious neurologic compromise. Consider four broad categories: nonspecific low back pain; radicular pain; spinal-stenosis pattern; and back pain associated with a serious condition such as cauda equina syndrome, infection, fracture, malignancy, inflammatory disease, vascular pathology, or visceral disease.

Most acute low back pain is nonspecific and improves over time. That does not make the visit trivial. Pain severity, impaired function, fear, sleep disruption, depression, work demands, caregiving, prior trauma, substance use, medication safety, and access to physical therapy determine whether recovery is feasible.

Part 2 — Red Flags and Emergency Referral

Ask directly about new urinary retention or overflow incontinence, fecal incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bilateral progressive leg weakness, severe/progressive neurologic deficit, fever, immunosuppression, IV drug use, recent bacteremia/infection, major trauma, osteoporosis or prolonged corticosteroid exposure, history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, night/rest pain, and abdominal/vascular symptoms. The meaning of a red flag comes from the total pattern, not a checklist alone.

Possible cauda equina syndrome, rapidly progressive weakness, spinal epidural infection, cord/conus compression, unstable fracture, or vascular emergency warrants immediate emergency evaluation. Do not tell a patient with new saddle anesthesia and urinary retention to wait for the next available outpatient MRI. Safety and timely specialist/emergency assessment come first.

Part 3 — Focused History and Examination

Clarify onset, trauma, location, radiation, triggers, positional features, walking tolerance, relief with rest/flexion, fever/systemic symptoms, cancer/infection risks, bowel/bladder symptoms, numbness, weakness, falls, pregnancy possibility, and effect on work, sleep, mood, and daily activity. Perform a focused neurologic and musculoskeletal exam: gait, posture, range of motion, strength, sensation, reflexes, straight-leg or other provocation findings when appropriate, hip examination, vascular/perfusion clues, abdominal examination when indicated, and documentation of any objective deficit.

Radicular pain may include dermatomal pain or paresthesia. A stenosis pattern often has walking/standing limitation relieved by flexion or sitting. These are clues, not automatic diagnoses; hip disease, peripheral neuropathy, PAD, venous disease, and other causes can coexist.

Part 4 — Imaging Stewardship: Ask a Question

For acute low back pain without focal neurologic deficits or red flags, routine imaging generally does not improve outcomes and can expose patients to incidental findings, cost, anxiety, and downstream intervention. Obtain imaging and appropriate laboratory testing when there are serious/progressive neurologic deficits, concern for infection/fracture/cancer/other serious pathology, persistent symptoms when results would change management, or a planned invasive intervention. Select modality and urgency to match the clinical question and consult when needed.

Explain this to patients clearly: “We are not ignoring the pain; the exam does not currently show a reason that immediate imaging is likely to help, and we have a plan for recovery and return precautions.” This is safer than either reflexive imaging or dismissing the concern.

Part 5 — Functional Recovery and Nonpharmacologic Care

Set functional goals: walking to the mailbox, sleeping more comfortably, returning to work safely, or caring for a child. Encourage activity within tolerance and avoidance of prolonged bed rest when no emergency condition is suspected. Options may include education, heat, structured exercise/physical therapy, movement-based therapies, cognitive behavioral approaches, mindfulness-based strategies, and multidisciplinary rehabilitation according to the clinical presentation, preference, availability, and current evidence.

Psychosocial factors can predict disability and persistent pain. Ask about fear avoidance, catastrophizing, trauma, depression, anxiety, job demands, housing, food security, language, and access. This is not “the pain is all psychological”; it is recognition that pain, function, nervous-system sensitization, and recovery are biopsychosocial.

Part 6 — Medication and Opioid Safety

Medication can be an adjunct, not the whole plan. Match therapy to pain pattern, comorbidities, kidney/liver/GI/cardiovascular risk, pregnancy potential, drug interactions, fall risk, sedation, substance-use history, and patient goals. Avoid duplicative NSAID exposure and reconcile OTC products. Muscle relaxants, neuropathic-pain agents, antidepressants, topical options, and analgesics have different roles and risks; use current guidance and avoid indefinite continuation without evidence of functional benefit.

Opioids require exceptional caution because risks include sedation, falls, respiratory depression, overdose, constipation, tolerance, and use disorder. They are not a default solution for nonspecific low back pain. If a patient is already receiving opioids, do not abruptly discontinue medication through a routine portal instruction; reassess benefit/risk, safety, comorbid mental-health/substance-use needs, and use a patient-centered plan with appropriate support.

Part 7 — Referral and Follow-Up

Refer or collaborate when there are red flags, progressive objective deficits, functionally disabling symptoms despite appropriate care, uncertain diagnosis, significant psychosocial complexity, potential interventional/surgical question, or medication/pain-management complexity. Close the loop on imaging, labs, therapy, work forms, and return precautions. Persistent pain deserves reassessment of the diagnosis and recovery plan—not simply another refill.

Clinical Case

A 58-year-old with diabetes presents with new severe back pain, fever, and progressive leg weakness after a recent skin infection. The patient has difficulty walking.

FNP reasoning: fever, recent infection, and progressive neurologic deficit raise concern for spinal infection or compression. This is not uncomplicated mechanical back pain and is not appropriate for delayed conservative outpatient management. Arrange immediate emergency evaluation and communicate the neurologic/infectious concern.

FNP Low Back Pain Framework

  1. Screen for danger: neurologic emergency, infection, fracture, malignancy, inflammatory/vascular/visceral concern.
  2. Characterize the pattern: nonspecific, radicular, stenosis-like, or other; assess function and trajectory.
  3. Examine with purpose: gait, strength, sensation, reflexes, provocation, hips, and relevant systemic findings.
  4. Use testing selectively: image/lab when a result will address a serious condition or change management.
  5. Support recovery: meaningful functional goals, active nonpharmacologic care, medication safety, follow-up, and referral when needed.

High-Yield Summary

First task: exclude serious neurologic and systemic causes before labeling pain as mechanical.
Emergency signs: saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, progressive weakness, severe systemic/infectious signs, or unstable trauma/vascular concern.
Imaging: is not routine for uncomplicated acute low back pain without red flags or focal deficits.
Recovery: centers on function, activity within tolerance, education, and individualized nonpharmacologic care.
Medication: requires comorbidity, interaction, fall/sedation, and opioid-risk assessment.
FNP standard: avoid both missed emergencies and unnecessary imaging while helping the patient function safely.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Low-back-pain examination, imaging, medication selection, opioid management, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, collaboration/scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
